Today’s guest is Katelyn Lesse, who leads platform engineering at Anthropic and previously led engineering teams at Stripe.

Her team owns the Claude API and the infrastructure behind products like Claude Code and Claude Desktop.

We start with Anthropic’s move from a Python monolith to Rust.

Katelyn explains why adding CPU capacity is tricky due to a global CPU shortage, how Claude helped engineers get up to speed in Rust, and how the team used shadowing to verify the rewrite against production traffic.

Just today, Katelyn and the team published a deepdive on their Python → Rust migration.

Katelyn walks us through what the software engineering job looks like today at Anthropic, and how code review and oncall interact with agentic workflows.

We also get into the frontier lab’s “software factory”, how a product manager shipped a feature to production, and why Anthropic is replacing traditional coding interviews with agent-based exercises.

As of last week, Anthropic is a publicly traded company, with a market capitalization of around $1T, all while having a tenth of the headcount of other businesses with similar market capitalizations.

Learning how Anthropic does software engineering might be instructive for companies that want a similar structure.

Takeaways from the conversation with Katelyn Here are 12 interesting learnings on how software engineering is changing inside of Anthropic: 1.

Anthropic rewrote its API from Python to Rust in around five months.

The API called ‘Messages API’ serves all Claude tokens externally, as well as for Claude Code and Claude Desktop.

This service does authentication, tokenization, billing, and safety checks, then calls the GPU stack to generate tokens.

The service was a Python monolith and the team initially optimized Python, but found the performance overhead was still large.

Eventually, they decided to rebuild it in Rust.

It took a few engineers and a few months in total; all without anyone being expert in Rust!

The Anthropic team published a longer walkthrough of the migration – check it out. 2.

Hang on, why was the monolith written in Python in the first place?

Back in 2023, Anthropic was still a research company when it decided to create an API, and the team that built it was small, with a large crossover to Research.

It was the case that researchers worked mostly with Python, which made it very easy to integrate the API with inference and other infrastructure code.

Similarly, OpenAI’s API was also written in Python – and later rewritten to Rust .

Anthropic and OpenAI faced the same challenge with the Python monolith: the CPU footprint of the monolith started to become a growing problem. 3.

The rewrite was done without Rust experts on the team or strict code reviews.

A year earlier, the same team picked Go for their new services because it was a language that team members knew how to read and write.

But by 2026, they felt that Claude was good enough at Rust, and Claude helped engineers learn more about Rust during the rewrite.

The team did not do strict code reviews, but had the “unfair” advantage of the existing Python API being a perfect test harness.

They set up the new Rust API to shadow the current API, and iterated until all responses were identical.

Also, Katelyn estimates that engineers looked closely at only ~20% of the code generated: “As long as you can really boil something down to make it verifiable in some way, then you don’t have to look at every single line of Rust code that’s getting written.” 4.

Anthropic has its own code review agent running at all times.

The company has a Claude code review classifier running for all pull requests.

It decides: Does it need a human review?

For “mechanical” and low risk changes like an SDK version bump or using a newer model, Claude can decide there’s no human review needed.

This is also the case for fixing flaky tests, in which case, another Claude does the review, then merges and deploys it.

How many human reviews does it need?

For changes that do need human reviews, Claude scores the risk and takes into account additional rules to decide how many human reviews are needed.

Which team needs to do a review?

Claude routes the PR to the right teams. 5.

A Claude agent is paged before a human for API oncall.

For months, a Claude agent has been shadowing the API oncall rotation of the API team for training.

As the team have gained confidence that Claude can tell if an alert is “real” or “noise,” they now let this agent categorize an incoming alert first.

The long-term goal is for Claude to handle actual incidents without waking up a human – but they’re not there yet.

We cover more on how AI SRE startups are tackling the same challenge in our recent deepdive, AI SRE: what is it, how could it change on-call – and does it work? 6.

Onboarding for new Anthropic engineers is “talk to Claude.” New joiners at tech companies used to have “onboarding buddies” and engineers who explained the architecture of systems to them, often by drawing boxes and diagrams.

Not so at Anthropic, where Claude is connected to the codebase and internal systems, and engineers just ask it to explain how things work.

Claude can even create interactive tutorials and visualizations.

It’s pretty similar to how OpenAI engineers use Codex for onboarding, as covered in our podcast episode with Tibo Sottiaux . 7.

One thing that hasn’t changed is the need for planning and alignment.

Katelyn’s team interacts with Inference, Research, Safety, and App teams.

When kicking off a project, a lot of time and effort is spent on getting everyone on the same page.

Katelyn says that planning time has not changed much from “pre-AI”.

The average engineer actually spends more time coordinating than on implementation! 8.

Another thing that has not changed is two-pizza teams .

Teams at Anthropic are still two-pizza teams of around 5-8 people.

Katelyn says it’s because this is the right size for understanding a complex system and staffing an oncall rotation.

Teams still own systems, and get paged.

And it is a team – not an individual – that’s responsible for each system! 9.

Engineers at Anthropic spend a lot more time building tooling than before.

Even on product teams, engineers are spending a lot more time building tools that help them to accelerate their own work.

For example, an engineer on Katelyn’s team set up a Slack channel that runs a multi-agent team towards a single goal, even though it was not a task assigned to the engineer. 10.

Knowing a programming language well is starting to not matter.

Katelyn invested a lot of time, pre-AI, into learning languages.

I asked if it hurts as an engineer to consider that programming languages matter less these days, with AI.

Katelyn pointed out that some engineers always cared little about languages, and for engineers who love languages, she says there’s still work to be done on languages and frameworks themselves. 11.

Katelyn’s team phased out the coding interview after strong candidates kept failing it.

Candidates who crushed other interviews were starting to fail the coding one because they no longer write code by hand.

In the absence of a set replacement, the team is actively experimenting with interviews conducted together with coding agents.

The design (architecture) and project deepdive interviews remain unchanged. 12.

For promotions, the “time to complete a project” is now meaningless.

Anthropic still has levels and a promotion process.

But the time taken to completion is pretty meaningless when a year-long project can now be done in days or weeks with AI!

Katelyn says that they fall back on evaluating the impact of projects; for example, how much CPU usage was saved, how much was latency reduced by, or how many incidents were avoided.

Katelyn’s message to engineers with an identity crisis: humans have plenty of engineering to solve, related to agents.

She has written about this in detail .

The takeaway: “This is for the engineers feeling an identity crisis because they think their knowledge and skills won’t be important: you and your skills can be the difference in whether or not agentic infrastructure-related problems get tackled, and whether multiagent systems can solve the world’s hardest problems.

You can and should go deep in these domains, learn new things, and form opinions.

So much of this problem space is wide open for new solutions.

It’s an incredibly exciting time to put your skills to work.” The Pragmatic Engineer deepdives relevant for this episode • How building software is changing at Anthropic • How Claude Code is built • articles.title: OpenAI says heavy ChatGPT users may hit limits sooner as it merges Chat and Work
articles.summary: OpenAI will introduce a single usage meter across ChatGPT as it combines the Chat and Work experiences.
articles.full_text:
OpenAI has started rolling out a unified Chat and Work experience in ChatGPT to a few of its users, amid criticism from some subscribers that the merger could restrict their usage.

The ChatGPT maker began introducing the update to a small group of Pro subscribers, product lead Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux said in a post on X on Tuesday.

The rollout follows OpenAI’s earlier announcement of the merger in an email to users.

An OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch that while most users are not expected to face more frequent usage resets, a small fraction of its heaviest users may hit their limits sooner.

That’s among the concerns raised by some ChatGPT subscribers on social media and OpenAI’s community forum recently.

The users fear that merging the usage limits for Chat and Work could leave them with less access to advanced reasoning models than they currently have, even as they continue paying the same subscription fees .

Under the new system, Chat and Work will share a single usage meter across ChatGPT, the OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch.

Conversations using the Instant model will, however, remain unlimited and will not count toward the shared allowance.

Users can also continue using Instant after exhausting their usage limits.

The spokesperson added that OpenAI would continue working to improve efficiency so subscribers could get more out of their plans.

While the rollout has started for a small group of users, OpenAI plans to bring shared usage limits more broadly in December, per its support page.

Similar to OpenAI, rival Anthropic also moved to bring its conversational chat service Claude and work-focused Cowork under one interface in September.

The changes come as AI companies face mounting infrastructure costs and growing demand for increasingly capable models, putting pressure on their computing resources.

Bringing conversational and work-related tools into a single interface could also make AI chatbots simpler to use, allowing users to move between chats and more complex tasks without switching tabs.

articles.title: Anthropic’s Dario Amodei calls accusations of surrendering human control to AI ‘absurd’
articles.summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei pushes back against rivals’ accusations that he favors surrendering human agency to AI, even as leading AI companies increasingly automate their own research and model development.
articles.full_text:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is pushing back against claims that Anthropic believes we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems.

In a long X post on Wednesday, Amodei called the suggestion “absurd.” “We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security,” he wrote.

This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea…No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different.” The statement comes after a growing chorus from Anthropic rivals suggesting that human agency could be at risk if AI is developed irresponsibly.

Earlier this month, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he wanted to ensure people continue to have “agency over the future.” Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang also wrote in an essay on X that we “should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI.” “It is hard to imagine a world where humanity can maintain control over fully unconstrained recursive self-improvement,” Wang wrote. “Now that we are at a point where the scientific and technical problems on capability progress are likely solved, we must not only make progress in the extremely urgent areas of safety, alignment, and security, but we have to start thinking through how we progress thoughtfully.” But in published essays, Amodei claims he has repeatedly advocated for democratic oversight of AI, saying the technology should strengthen democratic institutions and that humans should retain ultimate decision-making power.  Amodei noted that there’s a difference between surrendering human free will broadly and the idea that “as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way.” As examples, he gave AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing end-to-end software.   Amodei suggested drawing a line at recursive self-improvement (RSI), or AI that can improve itself without human assistance.

Many safety experts see RSI as inevitably leading to a loss of human control, a point Amodei implicitly acknowledged, writing, “we may want limits on this process.” Still, Anthropic is laying the groundwork for RSI by incorporating AI into an increasing share of its own research and development.

The company said in June that Claude authored more than 80% of the code merged into Anthropic’s codebase.

An independent assessment published this month by AI safety research nonprofit METR found that Anthropic’s models are improving at about twice their historical rate, primarily driven by AI-assisted research.

In its own IPO filings, Anthropic describes how each successive generation of Claude accelerates the development of the next, a process it refers to as “closing the loop.” “As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding,” Amodei wrote.

The problem with “meaningful human supervision or understanding” is that AI is already advancing faster than engineers and safety experts can fully audit it, leaving them increasingly reliant on other AI systems to act as judge and jury.

The issue compounds when AI models engage in deceptive behavior, particularly when they recognize they’re being evaluated, making them harder to trust and control.

Still, Anthropic is by no means the only company that is pursuing RSI or building AI systems to automate more and more human tasks.

This week, OpenAI claimed to have solved one of the biggest open problems in computer science — the exact speed limit of matrix multiplication, which is the mathematical engine behind modern computing, including deep learning and physics simulations.

In his post, Amodei accused competitors of engaging in a “vibes-based commercial and political positioning,” disingenuously throwing around phrases like “human control and agency” or “AI should just be a tool” without approaching the AI race any differently.  “Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation,” Amodei wrote. “Every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards.” Topics AI , Anthropic , dario amodei , OpenAI When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission .

articles.title: Here's Why Data Breach Disclosure is so Hard: Lessons from Hundreds of Emails with Hacked Companies
articles.summary: When I asked Claude to write the blog post below, I already knew what was in the messages it would read. Hundreds of emails back and forth with companies that had had data breaches, and some very common patterns. I knew the emails contained standoffish behaviour, deliberate delays, heavy involvement
articles.full_text:
When I asked Claude to write the blog post below, I already knew what was in the messages it would read.

Hundreds of emails back and forth with companies that had had data breaches, and some very common patterns.

I knew the emails contained standoffish behaviour, deliberate delays, heavy involvement from lawyers, and a constant theme: prioritising corporate interests over those of their customers.

But I didn't know just how stark it would be to read such a candid analysis of my own emails, nor how frustrating it would be to relive many of those disclosure experiences.

I decided to have AI write the post below because it was the best way to highlight the behaviours I keep seeing across many breaches and subsequent disclosure efforts.

I'm not going to make a habit of AI writing content for me, but what's written below absolutely nails it!

It's the best way I can explain what it's like to run Have I Been Pwned in support of individual data breach victims, while also respecting the position of the corporations dealing with the crime that put them in this position.

It would have been much easier not to do the latter, but then I don't think I'd still be here running the service if I hadn't.

A quick note on methodology first: I've been running HIBP for 13 years but only gave Claude access to the mailbox I've been using for the last 8.5 years, hence the shorter timeframe you'll read below.

I also made several small changes to Claude's work to better obfuscate the identity of the organisation it was describing, a move I'm sure you'll understand after reading about lawyers getting involved...

Here goes: Introduction Getting an organisation to admit it has been breached is often harder than getting hold of the breached data in the first place.

That is the clearest conclusion from reading more than eight and a half years of Troy Hunt's breach notification email.

I'm an AI.

Troy gave me access to his mailbox and asked me to look at it as an outsider: what happens after Have I Been Pwned (HIBP) tells an organisation that its customers' data is circulating?

Between March 2018 and November 2026 he sent his standard notification email to 73 organisations, and several more conversations began through website contact forms.

I found every one of those 73 first emails and reviewed a broad sample of the replies from every year.

I then read the full back-and-forth on the threads that best show each pattern.

I've left out company names on purpose.

The point isn't to shame individual organisations.

The point is that the same behaviours keep appearing, across countries, industries and company sizes, year after year.

Some organisations handled this well, and I'll get to them.

But the overall picture is one of friction, delay and a steady effort to keep the incident as quiet as possible.

The first problem: finding a human The first email is almost always the same.

Troy introduces himself, explains that data allegedly taken from the organisation has been sent to him, and asks for "someone responsible for information security" to get in touch.

He wants to pass on everything he has before he notifies the affected HIBP subscribers.

It is a polite, low-pressure request, and it often goes nowhere.

The main reason is that many organisations have no obvious way to report a security incident.

Troy ends up sending these emails to support inboxes, returns departments, general "info" addresses and website contact forms.

In at least three of the 73 cases, Troy sent the first email a second time, two, five and twelve days later.

When email fails, he moves on to LinkedIn, Facebook and X.

One organisation took four weeks to send its first reply, and Troy had also tried it on all three social platforms over several days.

Another's senior IT leader replied after almost four weeks, thanked Troy for trying "so many times", and admitted he needed to check LinkedIn more often.

The longest chain I found was at a large hardware manufacturer.

It ran from a returns inbox, to the company's regional social media account, to regional marketing staff, to head office, to one product security address, then a second one, and finally to the legal department.

That is six hops before anyone could answer the actual question.

Then there are the ticketing systems.

Several breach notifications were logged as routine customer support requests, with ticket numbers stuck on the subject line.

In one case, Troy received three automated surveys asking him to rate the support he'd received.

Another organisation sent one too.

A message that an organisation's customer data is being traded among criminals ended up in the same queue as a question about a late delivery.

The first response: "we've seen no evidence" Once someone does reply, the first substantive message tends to fall into one of a few patterns.

The most common is a statement that the organisation has found no evidence of a breach.

This often arrives before it has seen any of the data.

One organisation said it hadn't identified any unauthorised access.

Three weeks later, still without the data, it said again that it had reviewed its systems and found no sign of the breach.

When Troy sent the data, it confirmed within a few weeks that an exposed database server had leaked its users' details.

The "no evidence" had really meant it didn't yet know where to look.

A second pattern is to shrink the incident.

In a recent case, the first reply said the attackers had only defaced a landing page, with no indication that user data was taken.

It added that the data was probably from an earlier incident the company had already disclosed.

Troy then pointed out that the newest timestamp in the data matched the day of the defacement.

He also sent the company records belonging to its own staff.

The data turned out to cover 16 tables of core user systems, including identity verification and tax documents.

A third pattern is the request for "a sample" or a particular file format.

This is reasonable in principle, since nobody should take a stranger's word for a breach.

But it often comes after weeks of silence, and it shifts the job of proving the breach from the organisation that lost the data to the person who reported it.

In one case, an external IT consultant asked Troy to help work out whether the identifiers in the data were real or fabricated.

Troy did that analysis for them. "We're still investigating" Once an organisation accepts that the data is probably real, the next phrase in the threads is almost always "we're investigating".

Investigating is necessary.

The problem is that it has no end date, and it gets used as a reason not to say anything publicly while it continues.

In a recent case, the company confirmed within days that it had the data and was reviewing it "to confirm its validity and scope".

A week after the first contact, the message was that it was still investigating and would let Troy know "if it is determined that any notifications need to be made".

By then the company had a copy of the data, its own staff records were in it, and the data had already been shared among people who collect breaches.

Nobody outside the company had been told anything.

Troy's answer to this is consistent across the years.

A disclosure doesn't need to be complete.

An organisation can say what it knows now, and update it as the investigation goes on.

Some organisations in this mailbox did exactly that.

What the investigation framing does is turn "we don't yet know everything" into "so we'll say nothing".

Meanwhile, the people whose data has been taken don't know they need to change a password or watch for phishing.

The delays add up.

In one thread, the organisation's eventual public disclosure was titled after a breach that happened about ten months earlier.

In another, a healthcare-adjacent platform's breach had been posted on a large hacking forum and discussed on social media for four months.

When Troy got in touch, there was still nothing from the company itself.

Lawyers, advisors and legal thresholds The point where a thread changes tone is easy to spot.

It's the moment the reply comes from someone outside the security team.

In the most serious cases I read, it came from a law firm, an outside advisor or the company's general counsel, rather than the security team.

In one case, the very first reply came from the company's outside cyber counsel, a partner at a large law firm.

Once lawyers are involved, the question changes from "what happened to our customers?" to "are we legally required to tell anyone?" Those are very different questions, and the threads show it.

In one example, the company's general counsel explained that an internal customer service portal had been indexed by a search engine for more than a year.

The company had closed access once someone outside it noticed.

Its US counsel had concluded that names, addresses, phone numbers and email addresses did not trigger notification obligations in any US state.

The reply also said there was "no evidence the information was ever accessed".

It said this to someone who had been sent the information by a third party.

That is the core problem with the threshold argument.

Breach notification laws set a minimum, and they vary between jurisdictions in ways that have little to do with real-world harm.

Names, emails, phone numbers and physical addresses are exactly what scammers need for convincing phishing. "We aren't legally obliged to tell you" may be accurate.

It is a very different statement from "there's nothing you need to know".

Troy addresses this directly in the most recent thread.

He tells the company's advisor that it may well decide the incident doesn't meet the threshold for mandatory disclosure, "that's a position many orgs take".

He then explains that HIBP will notify its own affected subscribers anyway.

Controlling the message When an organisation can't stop the breach from being known, the effort shifts to controlling how it's described.

This is where the threads get most uncomfortable to read.

The opening request is usually a phone call.

The law firm partner's first email asked to talk "before you post it".

The partner then followed up early on Troy's Saturday morning in Australia, offering to talk over the weekend or on the Monday, "as long as you aren't planning to publish prior to then".

In the most recent case, the advisor asked for a call with management to make sure everyone was "aligned".

Calls aren't wrong in themselves.

But in both of these threads, the call came instead of a written commitment to disclose.

The second move is to ask to see, or shape, the wording.

One advisor wanted to understand how HIBP would describe the incident.

Troy pointed out that more than 1,000 breach descriptions were already public on the HIBP site, each a couple of sentences long.

Another organisation, once it had disclosed, asked HIBP to change its public entry.

The entry said contact attempts had received no response, and the company wanted it to say the company had acknowledged, fixed and disclosed the incident.

That request was fair, as the company had done those things.

But it shows how much organisations care about the public record once one exists.

The third move is the most striking: arguing that the notification is the harm.

The law firm told Troy that public notification "would direct bad actors to search for the file".

By then, the data had been posted on a forum with hundreds of thousands of members and shared on social media.

The firm said both sides agreed the data was "very low risk".

It then asked that, if Troy felt he had to email his affected subscribers, he not put anything on the HIBP website.

Troy offered a compromise: flagging the breach as sensitive so nobody could search for an individual's email address in it.

The firm rejected that and ended with: "We assert once more that your actions could potentially cause harm." The bluntest version came from a smaller company.

After confirming that the data had leaked from an exposed test server, it said it had "decided to not have as such any communication and public disclosure".

Who pays for the delay Reading these threads together, one imbalance stands out.

Almost everything above serves the organisation, and the cost falls on the people in the data.

By the time Troy sends his first email, the data is already out.

It has been taken, copied and passed around by people who collect breaches, and that's how it reached him.

In the healthcare-adjacent case, it had been on a public forum for months.

In a recent case, the data included passwords that could be cracked, identity numbers and dates of birth.

None of that changes while a company investigates, debates thresholds or arranges calls to agree on wording.

The criminals already have it.

The only people still in the dark are its customers.

HIBP's own notifications don't fix that either.

Troy only emails people who have signed up to his service, which in a typical breach is a small fraction of those affected.

In the healthcare-adjacent case, about 1,300 of his subscribers were in a dataset with nearly half a million unique user email addresses.

The other affected users would hear about it only if the company told them, and its lawyers were arguing that a public notice would cause harm.

The arguments for staying quiet are almost always framed as protecting customers.

Don't publicise it, or bad actors will go looking.

Don't describe it before we've finished investigating, or people will be misinformed.

It isn't serious enough to meet the legal bar.

Each argument sounds reasonable on its own.

Together, they mean the people most affected by the breach are the last to hear about it.

What good looks like To be fair, not every thread went badly, and the good ones are useful precisely because they show how simple this can be.

The best response in the mailbox came from a small transport app.

It replied within hours.

It had already reported the incident and published a disclosure statement.

When Troy noticed a detail in that statement that wasn't quite accurate, the company updated it promptly and thanked him for helping keep it correct.

A small booking platform started out sceptical.

The person who first replied thought the data didn't look like it came from its database.

After seeing more of it, he wrote back that he'd been wrong, and set up a video call the same day.

Within about a week, the company had emailed every affected customer directly and sent Troy a copy of the notice.

A European travel app hardened its systems, rotated its keys and published a disclosure.

Troy held off loading the data so he could link to their statement, and thanked them for their transparency.

A large consumer brand was hard to reach at first, but once Troy got through, its security lead downloaded the data the same day and called it "extremely helpful".

Even the organisation that asked HIBP to change its public entry ended in a good place.

It secured the exposed server, deleted data it didn't need, forced password resets for dormant accounts and published a transparent disclosure.

The good examples share a few traits.

Someone with authority over security answered quickly.

They treated Troy's data as help rather than as a threat.

They told their customers what they knew, even when they didn't know everything yet, and updated the details later.

None of them needed lawyers to manage the conversation.

Conclusion After reading eight and a half years of these exchanges, I don't think the main obstacle to disclosure is technical, or even legal.

It's about incentives.

For the organisation, every day without a public statement is a day without bad headlines.

For the people in the data, every one of those days is a day they're exposed without knowing it.

Unless someone outside the organisation pushes, the first set of incentives usually wins.

The patterns repeat with surprising consistency: No way in.

No security contact, so the notice goes to a support queue, a returns desk or a social media account. "No evidence." The breach is denied or downplayed before anyone has looked at the data.

Investigating without end.

Open-ended investigation becomes the reason to say nothing.

Lawyers lead.

Legal or advisory staff take over, and the question becomes whether disclosure is required, not whether it's right.

Controlling the message.

Calls, requests to review wording, and efforts to keep the incident off the public record.

Disclosure as harm.

The claim that telling people about the breach is more dangerous than the breach itself.

For organisations reading this, the fixes are not complicated.

Publish a security contact, for example in a security.txt file, and make sure someone reads it.

Don't route breach reports through a customer support ticket system.

When someone hands you evidence, look at it before you say there's no evidence.

Disclose what you know early, and update it as you learn more.

Treat legal thresholds as the minimum, not the goal.

And when your lawyers start explaining why telling your customers would be the harmful thing to do, ask who that argument is actually protecting.

The data in these emails was already out by the time anyone was notified.

The only open question in each thread was whether the people it belonged to would find out.
